docx_valid_fallback.text_content: Machine Learning Applications in Healthcare: A Comprehensive Review John Smith, Jane Doe Department of Computer Science, University of Technology School of Medicine, Medical University Abstract Machine learning has revolutionized healthcare by enabling predictive analytics, personalized treatment, and improved diagnostic accuracy. This paper provides a comprehensive review of machine learning applications in healthcare, covering supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and deep learning approaches. We examine recent advances in medical imaging, disease prediction, drug discovery, and patient monitoring. Our analysis reveals that machine learning models achieve high accuracy in various healthcare tasks, with deep learning showing particular promise in image-based diagnostics. However, challenges remain in data privacy, model interpretability, and clinical integration. We discuss future directions including federated learning, explainable AI, and real-time clinical decision support systems. Keywords:  machine learning; healthcare; deep learning; medical imaging; predictive analytics; clinical decision support I. INTRODUCTION Healthcare systems worldwide face increasing challenges in managing growing patient populations, rising costs, and the need for personalized treatment approaches. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a transformative technology that addresses these challenges by enabling data-driven decision making and automated pattern recognition in complex medical data. The application of machine learning in healthcare spans multiple domains including diagnostic imaging, disease prediction, treatment optimization, and patient monitoring. Recent advances in deep learning have particularly accelerated progress in medical image analysis, achieving performance comparable to or exceeding human experts in specific tasks. A. Motivation The motivation for this review stems from the rapid proliferation of ML applications in healthcare and the need for a comprehensive analysis of current capabilities, limitations, and future directions. Understanding the state of the art is crucial for researchers, clinicians, and policymakers. B. Contributions This paper makes the following contributions: (1) A systematic review of ML applications across healthcare domains, (2) Analysis of performance metrics and clinical validation studies, (3) Discussion of challenges and ethical considerations, (4) Identification of future research directions. II. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK Machine learning in healthcare builds upon decades of research in artificial intelligence, medical informatics, and clinical decision support systems. Early expert systems in the 1970s laid the groundwork for automated medical reasoning, while modern ML approaches leverage large datasets and computational power. A. Machine Learning Fundamentals Machine learning encompasses supervised learning (classification and regression), unsupervised learning (clustering and dimensionality reduction), and reinforcement learning. In healthcare, supervised learning dominates due to the availability of labeled medical data. B. Healthcare Data Sources Healthcare ML systems utilize diverse data sources including electronic health records (EHRs), medical imaging (X-rays, CT, MRI), genomic data, wearable sensor data, and clinical notes. Data quality, standardization, and privacy are critical considerations. III. MACHINE LEARNING APPLICATIONS This section reviews major application areas of machine learning in healthcare, organized by clinical domain and task type. A. Medical Imaging Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in medical image analysis. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) excel at detecting abnormalities in radiological images, identifying tumors, and segmenting anatomical structures. Studies show that deep learning models can match or exceed radiologist performance in specific tasks such as diabetic retinopathy detection and lung nodule classification. TABLE I. Disease Prediction Predictive models use patient data to forecast disease onset, progression, and outcomes. Random forests, gradient boosting, and neural networks are commonly employed for risk stratification and early warning systems. C. Drug Discovery ML accelerates drug discovery by predicting molecular properties, identifying drug targets, and optimizing compound structures. Deep learning models can screen millions of compounds in silico, significantly reducing time and cost. IV. CHALLENGES AND LIMITATIONS Despite significant progress, several challenges hinder widespread adoption of ML in healthcare. A. Data Privacy and Security Healthcare data is highly sensitive and subject to strict regulations (HIPAA, GDPR). Ensuring privacy while enabling ML model training requires techniques such as federated learning, differential privacy, and secure multi-party computation. B. Model Interpretability Deep learning models often function as black boxes, making it difficult for clinicians to understand and trust their predictions. Explainable AI (XAI) methods such as attention mechanisms, saliency maps, and SHAP values help address this limitation. C. Clinical Integration Integrating ML systems into clinical workflows requires careful consideration of usability, validation, and regulatory approval. Models must be robust, reliable, and aligned with clinical practice guidelines. V. FUTURE DIRECTIONS The future of ML in healthcare is promising, with several emerging trends and research directions. A. Federated Learning Federated learning enables collaborative model training across institutions without sharing raw data, addressing privacy concerns while leveraging diverse datasets. B. Multimodal Learning Integrating multiple data modalities (imaging, genomics, EHRs) can improve diagnostic accuracy and enable more comprehensive patient assessment. C. Real-time Clinical Decision Support Deploying ML models at the point of care can provide real-time recommendations, alerts, and decision support to clinicians, improving patient outcomes and reducing errors. VI. CONCLUSION Machine learning has demonstrated significant potential in transforming healthcare through improved diagnostics, personalized treatment, and predictive analytics. While challenges remain in data privacy, model interpretability, and clinical integration, ongoing research and technological advances continue to address these limitations. The future of healthcare will likely see increasing collaboration between ML systems and human clinicians, combining the strengths of both to deliver better patient care. ( Abstract ) Keywords— component ,  formatting ,  style ,  styling ,  insert ( key words ) Introduction ( Heading 1 ) This template must be used as a guideline for the format and structure of articles published in the proceedings of the International Conference on Education and Technology (ICET). Authors are required to comply with the prescribed writing rules and structure, including font type, font size, formatting of tables and figures, and citation style. The columns are interconnected, so text will automatically flow from the left column to the right column once the left column is filled. Since this template uses a two-column format (left and right), any explanation of methods that includes diagrams, flowcharts, or tables must be adjusted to fit within the column layout. Format: Preferred formats are JPEG, TIFF, or PNG. Quality: Figures must be clear, sharp, and not pixelated. Any text within the images must be legible. Separation: Original high-resolution files should often be submitted separately from the main manuscript file, especially for complex graphs. the content as a separate text file.  Complete all content and organizational editing before formatting. Please note  sections A-D below for more information on proofreading, spelling and grammar. Keep your text and graphic files separate until after the text has been formatted and styled. Do not use hard tabs, and limit use of hard returns to only one return at the end of a paragraph. Do not add any kind of pagination anywhere in the paper. Do not number text heads-the template will do that for you. Abbreviations  and Acronyms Define abbreviations and acronyms the first time they are used in the text, even after they have been defined in the abstract. Abbreviations such as IEEE, SI, MKS, CGS, sc, dc, and rms do not have to be defined. Do not use abbreviations in the title or heads unless they are unavoidable. Units Use  either  SI (MKS) or CGS as primary units. (SI units are encouraged.) English units may be used as secondary units (in parentheses). An exception would be the use of English units as identifiers in trade, such as “3.5-inch disk drive”. Avoid combining SI and CGS units, such as current in amperes and magnetic field in oersteds. This often leads to confusion because equations do not balance dimensionally. If you must use mixed units, clearly state the units for each quantity that you use in an equation. Do not mix complete spellings and abbreviations of units: “Wb/m2” or “webers per square meter”, not “webers/m2”.  Spell out units when they appear in text: “. . . a few henries”, not “. . . a few H”. Identif y applicable  funding agency  here.  If none, delete this text box . Use a zero before decimal points: “0.25”, not “.25”. Use “cm3”, not “cc”.  ( bullet list ) Equations The equations are an exception to the prescribed specifications of this template. You will need to determine whether or not your equation should be typed using either the Times New Roman or the Symbol font (please no other font). To create multileveled equations, it may be necessary to treat the equation as a graphic and insert it into the text after your paper is styled. Number equations consecutively. Equation numbers, within parentheses, are to position flush right, as in (1), using a right tab stop. To make your equations more compact, you may use the solidus ( / ), the exp function, or appropriate exponents. Italicize Roman symbols for quantities and variables, but not Greek symbols. Use a long dash rather than a hyphen for a minus sign. Punctuate equations with commas or periods when they are part of a sentence, as in : </w:r><w:r w:rsidR="008A2C7D" w:rsidRPr="00127EDD"><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Times New Roman" w:hAnsi="Times New Roman" w:cs="Times New Roman"/><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>a    b      </w:r><w:r w:rsidR="008A2C7D" w:rsidRPr="00CB66E6"><w:t>   Note that the equation is centered using a center tab stop. Be sure that the symbols in your equation have been defined before or immediately following the equation. Use “(1)”, not “Eq. (1)” or “equation (1)”, except at the beginning of a  sentence: “Equation (1) is . . .” Some Common Mistakes The word “data” is plural, not singular. The subscript for the permeability of vacuum   0 , and other common scientific constants, is zero with subscript formatting, not a lowercase letter “o”. In American  English, commas, semi colons, periods, question and exclamation marks are located within quotation marks only when a complete thought or name is cited, such as a title or full quotation. When quotation marks are used, instead of a bold or italic typeface, to highlight a word or phrase, punctuation should appear outside of the quotation marks. A parenthetical phrase or statement at the end of a sentence is punctuated outside of the closing parenthesis (like this). (A parenthetical sentence is punctuated within the parentheses.) A graph within a graph is an “inset”, not an “insert”. The word alternatively is preferred to the word “alternately” (unless you really mean something that alternates). Do not use the word “essentially” to mean “approximately” or “effectively”. In your paper title, if the words “that uses” can accurately replace the word “using”, capitalize the “u”; if not, keep using lower-cased. Be aware of the different meanings of the homophones “affect” and “effect”, “complement” and “compliment”, “discreet” and “discrete”, “principal” and “principle”. Do not confuse “imply” and “infer”. The prefix “non” is not a word; it should be joined to the word it modifies, usually without a hyphen. There is no period after the “et” in the Latin abbreviation “et al.”. The abbreviation “i.e.” means “that is”, and the abbreviation “e.g.” means “for example”. ( Abstract ) Keywords— component ,  formatting ,  style ,  styling ,  insert ( key words ) Introduction ( Heading 1 ) This template must be used as a guideline for the format and structure of articles published in the proceedings of the International Conference on Education and Technology (ICET). Authors are required to comply with the prescribed writing rules and structure, including font type, font size, formatting of tables and figures, and citation style. This template adopts a two-column format consisting of left and right columns. The columns are interconnected, so text will automatically flow from the left column to the right column once the left column is filled. Subheadings should be written using the provided styles (e.g.,  Heading 1 ) prepared by the committee. The introduction must include a general background, a review of previous studies (state of the art) to establish the scientific novelty of the article, a clear statement of the novelty, and the research problem (gap) or hypothesis. The final part of the introduction should present the objectives of the study and the limitations of the article. A separate literature review section is not required within the introduction. All manuscript content in each subsection must be written in Times New Roman, 10-point font, using A4 paper size (210 × 297 mm or 8.27” × 11.69”). All paragraphs, both in the left and right columns, must be justified. The article content must follow the template formatting rules with margins set to: top 1.9 cm, left 1.6 cm, right 1.6 cm, and bottom 2.56 cm. Paragraph spacing should be set as follows: left “0 pt”, right “0 pt”, before “0 pt”, and after “6 pt”. Method This section should explain the research in a chronological manner, including the research design, procedures, testing methods, and data collection techniques. The explanation may be supported by diagrams, flowcharts, or tables. The description of the research process must be supported by relevant references to ensure that it is scientifically acceptable. Since this template uses a two-column format (left and right), any explanation of methods that includes diagrams, flowcharts, or tables must be adjusted to fit within the column layout. Examples of the use of diagrams, flowcharts, and tables in explaining research methods can be seen in Figures 1 and 2 and Table 1. Figure captions should use the style  Fig. 1 , while tables should use the style  TABLE  I . Tables must be formatted using Times New Roman, 8-point font. For embedding images in the paper, authors are requested to follow the guidelines below: Minimum Resolution: Images (photographs, line drawings, maps) should have a minimum resolution of 300 DPI (dots per inch) for linework and 150-300 DPI for photographs. Format: Preferred formats are JPEG, TIFF, or PNG. Quality: Figures must be clear, sharp, and not pixelated. Any text within the images must be legible. Separation: Original high-resolution files should often be submitted separately from the main manuscript file, especially for complex graphs. No Screenshots: Images should not be taken from screenshots or print screens, as these usually lack the necessary resolution.   Example of a figure  caption . the content as a separate text file.  Complete all content and organizational editing before formatting. Please note  sections A-D below for more information on proofreading, spelling and grammar. Keep your text and graphic files separate until after the text has been formatted and styled. Do not use hard tabs, and limit use of hard returns to only one return at the end of a paragraph. Do not add any kind of pagination anywhere in the paper. Do not number text heads-the template will do that for you. Abbreviations  and Acronyms Define abbreviations and acronyms the first time they are used in the text, even after they have been defined in the abstract. Abbreviations such as IEEE, SI, MKS, CGS, sc, dc, and rms do not have to be defined. Do not use abbreviations in the title or heads unless they are unavoidable. Units Use  either  SI (MKS) or CGS as primary units. (SI units are encouraged.) English units may be used as secondary units (in parentheses). An exception would be the use of English units as identifiers in trade, such as “3.5-inch disk drive”. Avoid combining SI and CGS units, such as current in amperes and magnetic field in oersteds. This often leads to confusion because equations do not balance dimensionally. If you must use mixed units, clearly state the units for each quantity that you use in an equation. Do not mix complete spellings and abbreviations of units: “Wb/m2” or “webers per square meter”, not “webers/m2”.  Spell out units when they appear in text: “. . . a few henries”, not “. . . a few H”. Identif y applicable  funding agency  here.  If none, delete this text box . Use a zero before decimal points: “0.25”, not “.25”. Use “cm3”, not “cc”.  ( bullet list ) Equations The equations are an exception to the prescribed specifications of this template. You will need to determine whether or not your equation should be typed using either the Times New Roman or the Symbol font (please no other font). To create multileveled equations, it may be necessary to treat the equation as a graphic and insert it into the text after your paper is styled. Number equations consecutively. Equation numbers, within parentheses, are to position flush right, as in (1), using a right tab stop. To make your equations more compact, you may use the solidus ( / ), the exp function, or appropriate exponents. Italicize Roman symbols for quantities and variables, but not Greek symbols. Use a long dash rather than a hyphen for a minus sign. (1)” or “equation (1)”, except at the beginning of a  sentence: “Equation (1) is . . .” Some Common Mistakes The word “data” is plural, not singular. The subscript for the permeability of vacuum   0 , and other common scientific constants, is zero with subscript formatting, not a lowercase letter “o”. In American  English, commas, semi colons, periods, question and exclamation marks are located within quotation marks only when a complete thought or name is cited, such as a title or full quotation. When quotation marks are used, instead of a bold or italic typeface, to highlight a word or phrase, punctuation should appear outside of the quotation marks. A parenthetical phrase or statement at the end of a sentence is punctuated outside of the closing parenthesis (like this). (A parenthetical sentence is punctuated within the parentheses.) A graph within a graph is an “inset”, not an “insert”. The word alternatively is preferred to the word “alternately” (unless you really mean something that alternates). Do not use the word “essentially” to mean “approximately” or “effectively”. In your paper title, if the words “that uses” can accurately replace the word “using”, capitalize the “u”; if not, keep using lower-cased. Be aware of the different meanings of the homophones “affect” and “effect”, “complement” and “compliment”, “discreet” and “discrete”, “principal” and “principle”. Do not confuse “imply” and “infer”. The prefix “non” is not a word; it should be joined to the word it modifies, usually without a hyphen. There is no period after the “et” in the Latin abbreviation “et al.”. The abbreviation “i.e.” means “that is”, and the abbreviation “e.g.” means “for example”. An excellent style manual for science writers is [7]

Authors are required to comply with the prescribed writing rules and structure, including font type, font size, formatting of tables and figures, and citation style. This template adopts a two-column format consisting of left and right columns. The columns are interconnected, so text will automatically flow from the left column to the right column once the left column is filled. Subheadings should be written using the provided styles (e.g.,  Heading 1 ) prepared by the committee. The introduction must include a general background, a review of previous studies (state of the art) to establish the scientific novelty of the article, a clear statement of the novelty, and the research problem (gap) or hypothesis. The final part of the introduction should present the objectives of the study and the limitations of the article. A separate literature review section is not required within the introduction. All manuscript content in each subsection must be written in Times New Roman, 10-point font, using A4 paper size (210 × 297 mm or 8.27” × 11.69”). All paragraphs, both in the left and right columns, must be justified. The article content must follow the template formatting rules with margins set to: top 1.9 cm, left 1.6 cm, right 1.6 cm, and bottom 2.56 cm. Paragraph spacing should be set as follows: left “0 pt”, right “0 pt”, before “0 pt”, and after “6 pt”. Method This section should explain the research in a chronological manner, including the research design, procedures, testing methods, and data collection techniques. The explanation may be supported by diagrams, flowcharts, or tables. The description of the research process must be supported by relevant references to ensure that it is scientifically acceptable. Since this template uses a two-column format (left and right), any explanation of methods that includes diagrams, flowcharts, or tables must be adjusted to fit within the column layout. Examples of the use of diagrams, flowcharts, and tables in explaining research methods can be seen in Figures 1 and 2 and Table 1. Figure captions should use the style  Fig. 1 , while tables should use the style  TABLE  I . Tables must be formatted using Times New Roman, 8-point font. For embedding images in the paper, authors are requested to follow the guidelines below: Minimum Resolution: Images (photographs, line drawings, maps) should have a minimum resolution of 300 DPI (dots per inch) for linework and 150-300 DPI for photographs. Format: Preferred formats are JPEG, TIFF, or PNG. Quality: Figures must be clear, sharp, and not pixelated. Any text within the images must be legible. Separation: Original high-resolution files should often be submitted separately from the main manuscript file, especially for complex graphs. No Screenshots: Images should not be taken from screenshots or print screens, as these usually lack the necessary resolution.   Example of a figure  caption . w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="276" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:left="284" w:right="282"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:i/><w:iCs/><w:color w:val="000000"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00B10332"><w:rPr><w:i/><w:iCs/><w:color w:val="000000"/></w:rPr><w:t>The development of immersive technologies such as the metaverse and virtual reality has driven significant transformations in religious practices, including in the Islamic context. This article aims to analyze how Islamic religious practices are being reconfigured from physical to virtual spaces, and to evaluate their theoretical and normative implications. This research employs a qualitative approach with a critical literature review method, integrating the perspective of Jean Baudrillard's simulation theory and the virtual reality approach to digital religious studies.   The results of this study indicate that the metaverse not only functions as a new medium for da'wah (Islamic propagation) but also reshapes spiritual experiences through simulation processes that produce the phenomenon of hyperreality, where the boundaries between reality and representation become blurred. Practices such as virtual worship, avatar-based Islamic studies, and digital Muslim communities reflect a shift from a purely physical religious experience to a technologically mediated one. However, this transformation raises issues related to spiritual authenticity, the validity of Islamic jurisprudence ( fiqh ), and religious authority in the digital space.   From a normative Islamic perspective, particularly through the framework of the  maqāṣid  al- shari'ah  (the principles of Islamic law), this phenomenon presents both opportunities and challenges. The metaverse has the potential to expand access and inclusivity of global da'wah, but it also risks diminishing the sacred and embodied religiosity that are central to Islamic worship practices.   The novelty of this article lies in its synthesis of simulation theory and contemporary Islamic studies, proposing the concept of hyperreal Islamic ritual as a new analytical framework for understanding religious practices in the digital age. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="276" w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="005967E9"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>The development of digital technology over the past decade has been truly remarkable. It has significantly influenced a fundamental shift in the way humans interact, communicate, and construct meaning in life. In particular, the development and emergence of the metaverse and virtual reality (VR) have shaped the dynamics of digital technology. As Justin Thomas has explained, these developments have driven a fundamental transformation in patterns of human interaction from physical spaces toward immersive, interactive, and persistent digital spaces, thereby giving rise to new forms of social, cultural, and even religious experiences that no longer rely entirely on physical presence.   Meanwhile, in the Islamic tradition, religious practices possess a very distinctive characteristic: a strong connection between the spiritual and physical dimensions. Historically and normatively, they are deeply rooted in the physical and communal dimensions, such as congregational prayer in the mosque, the Hajj pilgrimage, and the transmission of knowledge through face-to-face gatherings, which emphasize the importance of embodied religiosity as an integral part of spiritual experience and collective piety. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="005967E9"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>However, the emergence of the metaverse as a next-generation digital space has begun to give rise to a new phenomenon: simulation-based religious practices, such as virtual worship through avatars, Islamic studies in three-dimensional environments, and simulations of religious rituals that transcend geographical and territorial boundaries.   Campbell adds that this transformation not only opens new opportunities for expanding access, inclusivity, and innovation in global da’wah, but also raises complex epistemological and normative issues, particularly regarding the authenticity of spiritual experiences, the validity of worship practices from a  fiqh  perspective, and the shift toward increasingly decentralized religious authority structures within a digital ecosystem governed by algorithms.   A number of recent studies indicate that while metaverse technology is generally accepted as  a tool for education and strengthening religious literacy, virtual religious practices have not yet fully gained legitimacy as a substitute for physical worship practices, as they are perceived to lack the dimensions of sacredness, existential presence, and spiritual depth that form the core of religious experience.   On the other hand, academic studies on the relationship between Islam and the metaverse are still dominated by descriptive approaches and have not yet extensively integrated critical theoretical frameworks, particularly the theory of simulation proposed by Jean Baudrillard, which, through the concepts of simulacra and hyperreality, explains how digital representations not only replicate reality but also have the potential to replace it and create experiences considered more real than reality itself. Within this framework, Islamic religious practices in virtual spaces have the potential to shift toward a form of hyperreal religiosity, in which the boundary between authentic spiritual experience and simulation becomes increasingly blurred and problematic. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="005967E9"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Against this backdrop, this article aims to provide a comprehensive and critical analysis of the transformation of Islamic religious practices from the physical to the virtual realm within the metaverse ecosystem by integrating perspectives from simulation theory and virtual reality approaches into the study of contemporary religion. More specifically, this study aims to: (1) identify and categorize forms of Islamic religious practices undergoing transformation within the metaverse; (2)  analyze  the implications of this phenomenon for the concepts of authenticity, spiritual experience, and the dimension of embodiment in Islam; (3) to evaluate the dynamics of change in religious authority and normative legitimacy within virtual worship practices; and (4) to formulate a new conceptual framework   hyperreal Islamic ritual   as a theoretical contribution to the development of Islamic studies in the digital age. Thus, this article aims not only to describe the phenomenon but also to offer a critical and constructive analysis capable of bridging the gap between Islamic normative traditions and global technological developments, while simultaneously opening up a space for multidisciplinary ijtihad that is adaptive to the challenges of the times. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/></w:rPr><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t>METHOD <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="005967E9"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>This study employs a qualitative approach using library research, focusing on a critical analysis of the phenomenon of the transformation of Islamic religious practices in the context of the development of metaverse and virtual reality technologies. A qualitative approach was chosen because it allows the researcher to deeply understand the meaning, social construction, and conceptual dynamics emerging within digital religious practices   aspects that cannot be measured quantitatively.  Within this framework, the study aims not only to describe the phenomenon but also to interpret and critically examine the epistemological and theological shifts arising from technological mediation. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="005967E9"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>The data sources for this study consist of secondary data obtained from various scholarly literature, including articles from reputable international journals, academic books, conference proceedings, and research reports relevant to the themes of the metaverse, virtual reality, digital religion, and contemporary Islamic studies. The selection of sources was conducted purposefully, taking into account credibility, relevance, and recency, to ensure they represent the latest developments in this field of study.  Additionally, classical and contemporary texts in Islamic studies were utilized to provide a normative foundation for  analyzing  religious practices. Data collection was conducted through documentary research by identifying, classifying, and categorizing literature directly related to the research focus. The collected data was then  analyzed  using content analysis combined with a critical hermeneutic approach. Content analysis is used to identify patterns, themes, and key concepts in the literature, while critical hermeneutics is used to interpret the meaning behind the text, particularly in understanding the relationship between technology, reality, and religious practices. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00932735"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">The analytical framework of this study integrates Jean Baudrillard’s theory of simulation with a virtual reality approach in the study of digital religion. The theory of simulation is used to explain how religious practices in the metaverse have  the potential to become forms of simulacra and hyperreality   that is, a condition in which digital representations no longer merely represent reality but actually replace it. Meanwhile, the virtual reality approach is used to understand how immersive experiences shape perceptions of presence and spiritual experiences in digital spaces.  The integration of these two approaches enables a comprehensive analysis of the ontological and phenomenological transformations in Islamic religious practices. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/></w:rPr></w:pPr></w:p><w:p w14:paraId="661DF3A5" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00325A61" w:rsidRDefault="00000000"><w:pPr><w:pBdr><w:top w:val="nil"/><w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/></w:rPr><w:t>DISCUSSION <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00932735"><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>The Metaverse and Virtual Reality: Concepts, Characteristics, and Ontological Implications <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00932735"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>The metaverse and virtual reality (VR) are two key concepts in contemporary digital technology that are fundamentally transforming the way humans understand, experience, and interact with reality. The term “metaverse” is derived from the words “ meta ” and “ universe ,” meaning a virtual world. It is generally understood as the next evolution of the internet toward an immersive digital space that enables simultaneous human interaction within a persistent, interconnected three-dimensional environment.  Unlike the conventional, two-dimensional screen-based internet, the metaverse offers an experience of “presence” within a digital space, where users not only access information but also “enter” and actively participate in the virtual world through avatar representations.  In a more comprehensive sense, the metaverse is a multi-user environment that integrates physical and virtual realities through the convergence of various technologies such as virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), artificial intelligence, and high-speed internet networks, thereby forming an immersive, interactive, and sustainable digital ecosystem. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00932735"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t>Meanwhile, virtual reality (VR) is a technology that allows individuals to experience a simulated digital environment that completely replaces physical reality through specific devices, such as special glasses, gloves, headsets, and motion sensors. VR works by creating a sense of presence—a psychological state in which users feel as though they are actually inside the virtual environment.   In this context, VR functions not only as a visualization tool but as an experiential medium capable of influencing users’ perceptions, emotions, and even their awareness of reality. Therefore, VR is often understood as a form of reality simulation with the capacity to reproduce, modify, and even create alternative realities that do not always have a direct counterpart in the physical world. The relationship between the metaverse and virtual reality is integrative, where VR serves as one of the key technologies enabling the realization of the metaverse as an immersive digital space. The metaverse can be understood as a macro-ecosystem or “digital universe,” while VR is one of the technological tools that allows individuals to access and experience that space in a profound way.   In other words, if VR is the gateway to virtual experiences, then the metaverse is the world where those experiences take place. In practice, the metaverse combines various technologies to create a digital environment that is not only immersive but also social, economic, and cultural, where users can interact, work, learn, and even live alternative lives in digital form. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00932735"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">The key characteristics of the metaverse encompass several important aspects.  First ,  immersiveness   the ability to create deep and realistic experiences through sensory integration.  Second , persistence   the continued existence of the virtual world even when users are not actively accessing it.  Third , interoperability   the ability to move between platforms while maintaining a consistent digital identity.  Fourth , social presence, which is the ability of users to interact in real-time with other users within a virtual space.  These characteristics make the metaverse not merely a simulated space, but an alternative reality with its own distinct social and cultural structures across all domains   including the economic sphere, where it  fosters independent economic activities such as property transactions and real-time buying and selling among group members; the social sphere, with its unique social cultural forms and designs; and the ability to create distinct communities, such as virtual mosques with all their activities, virtual religious study circles with their various topics, and so on. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="002656DC"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>From a philosophical perspective, the development of the metaverse and virtual reality carries significant ontological implications, particularly regarding the boundary between reality and representation. In the virtual world, human experience no longer depends entirely on the physical world, but rather on systematically designed digital constructs. This creates a situation where reality becomes fluid and can be continuously reproduced through technological simulations. In this context, virtual reality not only represents the real world but also has the potential to create a new world with its own logic, values, and experiences distinct from physical reality. Thus, the metaverse and virtual reality cannot be understood merely as technological innovations but as transformational phenomena that reshape paradigms regarding reality, presence, and human experience. Both open up new spaces for various aspects of life, including social, economic, educational, and religious dimensions, while simultaneously presenting new challenges regarding authenticity, identity, and the meaning of human existence in an increasingly complex digital age. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr></w:p><w:p w14:paraId="42632F89" w14:textId="286999AC" w:rsidR="00791536" w:rsidRPr="00791536" w:rsidRDefault="002656DC" w:rsidP="00791536"><w:pPr><w:pBdr><w:top w:val="nil"/><w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="002656DC"><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>Physical Presence in Worship: Between Ethics and Sacredness <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="002656DC"><w:t>Physical presence ( ḥuḍūr   jasadī ) in certain religious practices is regarded as an essential and inseparable element of authentic religious practice. Classical scholars assert that worship in Islam is an integration of the outward and inward dimensions, in which the involvement of the body serves as a crucial medium for fostering spiritual devotion; Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, in  Iḥyā ’ ‘ Ulūm  al- Dīn , emphasizes   <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:bidi/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Sakkal Majalla" w:hAnsi="Sakkal Majalla" w:cs="Sakkal Majalla"/><w:sz w:val="36"/><w:szCs w:val="36"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="000F0746"><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Sakkal Majalla" w:hAnsi="Sakkal Majalla" w:cs="Sakkal Majalla"/><w:sz w:val="36"/><w:szCs w:val="36"/><w:rtl/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">اعْلَمْ أَنَّ أَدِلَّةَ ذلك كثيرة فمن ذلك قوله تعالى أقم الصلاة لذكري وَظَاهِرُ الْأَمْرِ الْوُجُوبُ وَالْغَفْلَةُ تُضَادُّ الذِّكْرَ فَمَنْ غَفَلَ فِي جَمِيعِ صَلَاتِهِ كَيْفَ يَكُونُ مُقِيمًا لِلصَّلَاةِ  لِذِكْرِهِ وَقَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى وَلَا تَكُنْ مِنَ الغافلين نهي وظاهره التحريم وقوله عز وجل حتى تعلموا ما تقولون تَعْلِيلٌ لِنَهْيِ السَّكْرَانِ وَهُوَ مُطَّرِدٌ فِي الْغَافِلِ الْمُسْتَغْرِقِ الْهَمَّ بِالْوَسْوَاسِ وَأَفْكَارِ الدُّنْيَا وَقَوْلُهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إِنَّمَا الصَّلَاةُ تَمَسْكُنٌ وَتَوَاضُعٌ حَصْرٌ بِالْأَلِفِ وَاللَّامِ وَكَلِمَةِ إِنَّمَا لِلتَّحْقِيقِ وَالتَّوْكِيدِ وقد فهم الفقهاء من قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم إنما الشفعة فيما لم يقصر الحصر والإثبات والنفي وَقَوْلُهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مَنْ لَمْ تَنْهَهُ صَلَاتُهُ عَنِ الْفَحْشَاءِ وَالْمُنْكَرِ لَمْ يَزْدَدْ مِنَ اللَّهِ إِلَّا بُعْدًا وَصَلَاةُ الْغَافِلِ لَا تَمْنَعُ مِنَ الْفَحْشَاءِ وَالْمُنْكَرِ وَقَالَ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَمْ مِنْ قَائِمٍ حَظُّهُ مِنْ صَلَاتِهِ التَّعَبُ وَالنَّصَبُ (١) وَمَا أَرَادَ بِهِ إِلَّا الْغَافِلَ وَقَالَ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَيْسَ لِلْعَبْدِ مِنْ صَلَاتِهِ إِلَّا مَا عَقَلَ مِنْهَا (٢) وَالتَّحْقِيقُ فِيهِ أَنَّ الْمُصَلِّيَ مُنَاجٍ رَبَّهُ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ (٣) كَمَا وَرَدَ بِهِ الْخَبَرُ وَالْكَلَامُ مَعَ الغفلة ليس بمناجاة ألبتة وبيانه أن الزكاة إن غفل الإنسان عنها مثلاً فهي في نفسها مخالفة للشهوة شديدة على النفس وكذا الصوم قاهر للقوى كاسر لسطوة الهوى الذي هو آلة للشيطان عدو الله فلا يبعد أن يحصل منها مقصود مع الغفلة وكذلك الحج أفعاله شاقة شديدة وفيه من المجاهدة ما يحصل به <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="002656DC"><w:t>Based on Al-Ghazali’s explanation in the quote, spiritual presence ( ḥuḍūr  al- qalb ) is the essence of the quality and meaning of prayer, not merely an adjunct to the outward ritual. Al-Ghazali emphasizes that Allah’s command to perform prayer “to remember Him” indicates that the essence of prayer is conscious remembrance ( dhikr ), so that heedlessness ( ghaflah ) is actually contrary to the primary purpose of the act of worship itself. Prayer performed without awareness and the presence of the heart cannot be called true prayer, as it does not produce moral effects such as preventing evil and immoral deeds. In fact, he reinforces his argument with a hadith stating that a person only receives a portion of their prayer to the extent that they understand and perform it with full awareness. Therefore, according to al-Ghazali,  khusyuk  is not merely an additional spiritual aspect, but the primary substance that determines whether prayer truly becomes a form of  munajat  (dialogue) with Allah or merely empty physical movements devoid of meaning. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr></w:p><w:p w14:paraId="4B8F8268" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="002656DC" w:rsidRDefault="002656DC" w:rsidP="000F0746"><w:pPr><w:pBdr><w:top w:val="nil"/><w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr></w:p><w:p w14:paraId="63E4C505" w14:textId="61C811ED" w:rsidR="008A321E" w:rsidRDefault="002656DC" w:rsidP="002656DC"><w:pPr><w:pBdr><w:top w:val="nil"/><w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="002656DC"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">Physical movements in prayer, such as bowing and prostration, are not merely symbolic, but a means of bringing the heart to life. is of a  tawqīfī  nature and must be performed in accordance with the provisions of revelation, including the aspect of physical presence as part of its validity. Furthermore, in communal religious practice, physical presence serves a fundamental social function; Ibn Khaldun explains that <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:bidi/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Sakkal Majalla" w:hAnsi="Sakkal Majalla" w:cs="Sakkal Majalla"/><w:sz w:val="36"/><w:szCs w:val="36"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="0040453F"><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Sakkal Majalla" w:hAnsi="Sakkal Majalla" w:cs="Sakkal Majalla"/><w:sz w:val="36"/><w:szCs w:val="36"/><w:rtl/></w:rPr><w:t>وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ الْعَصَبِيَّةَ إِنَّمَا تَكُونُ مِنَ الِالْتِحَامِ بِالنَّسَبِ أَوْ مَا فِي مَعْنَاهُ، وَسَبَبُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ صِلَةَ الرَّحِمِ طَبِيعِيَّةٌ فِي الْبَشَرِ، وَهِيَ تُؤَدِّي إِلَى التَّنَاصُرِ وَالتَّعَاوُنِ <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00AE1028"><w:t>Direct interaction in collective activities such as congregational prayer and social visits plays a role in fostering social solidarity (‘ aṣabiyyah ), which forms the foundation of communal cohesion. Meanwhile, in the Islamic scholarly tradition, in-person study circles are regarded as the primary medium for the transmission of knowledge and etiquette; Ibn Jama’ah asserts that   <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:bidi/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Sakkal Majalla" w:hAnsi="Sakkal Majalla" w:cs="Sakkal Majalla"/><w:sz w:val="36"/><w:szCs w:val="36"/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00ED07CA"><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Sakkal Majalla" w:hAnsi="Sakkal Majalla" w:cs="Sakkal Majalla"/><w:sz w:val="36"/><w:szCs w:val="36"/><w:rtl/></w:rPr><w:t>وَيَنْبَغِي لِلطَّالِبِ أَنْ يَجْلِسَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْ شَيْخِهِ جِلْسَةَ الأَدَبِ وَالتَّوَاضُعِ، وَيُصْغِي إِلَيْهِ إِصْغَاءً تَامًّا، فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ أَقْرَبُ إِلَى الاِنْتِفَاعِ بِعِلْمِهِ <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00AE1028"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t>The blessings of knowledge are closely tied to the direct interaction between teacher and student, which enables the holistic transmission of values, ethics, and spirituality. In line with Al- Zarnuji’s  view <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:bidi/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Sakkal Majalla" w:hAnsi="Sakkal Majalla" w:cs="Sakkal Majalla"/><w:sz w:val="36"/><w:szCs w:val="36"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00ED07CA"><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Sakkal Majalla" w:hAnsi="Sakkal Majalla" w:cs="Sakkal Majalla"/><w:sz w:val="36"/><w:szCs w:val="36"/><w:rtl/></w:rPr><w:t>وَيَنْبَغِي أَنْ يَخْتَارَ الأُسْتَاذَ الأَعْلَمَ وَالأَوْرَعَ وَالأَسَنَّ، وَيَصْبِرَ عَلَى مُلَازَمَتِهِ وَخِدْمَتِهِ <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00AE1028"><w:t>which emphasizes the importance of companionship ( ṣuḥbah ) and close, intimate connection ( mulazamah ) in the learning process. Thus, physical presence is not merely a technical aspect but possesses fundamental theological, social, and epistemological dimensions; consequently, any transformation of religious practices into non-physical spaces must be critically examined, as it has the potential to shift the foundational structure of religious experience in Islam . <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr></w:p><w:p w14:paraId="71EC8808" w14:textId="5657C178" w:rsidR="00E85391" w:rsidRPr="00E85391" w:rsidRDefault="00AE1028" w:rsidP="00E85391"><w:pPr><w:pBdr><w:top w:val="nil"/><w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00AE1028"><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>The Transformation of Worship Spaces from Physical to Virtual <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00AE1028"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>The transformation of religious spaces from physical to virtual forms is one of the most significant implications of the development of metaverse and virtual reality technologies in contemporary religious life. Traditionally, in Islam, the mosque is understood not merely as a physical building, but as a sacred space that simultaneously integrates spiritual, social, and material dimensions. Physical presence within this space is an integral part of an embodied religious experience, where the body, space, and community interact as a unified religious experience. Thus, the mosque functions not only as a place of worship but also as a locus for the formation of the community’s collective identity and the internalization of spiritual values. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00AE1028"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>However, the emergence of the metaverse introduces a new paradigm in the form of virtual worship spaces that are immersive, interactive, and not bound by geographical boundaries. In this context, religious spaces are undergoing a process of dematerialization   a shift from concrete physical spaces toward digital spaces based on representation and simulation. The metaverse, as a persistent, multi-user virtual environment, allows individuals to “be present” in a space of worship without a physical body, but rather through a digital avatar that represents the user.   This phenomenon marks a fundamental shift in how religious practice is experienced, from one originally based on physical co-presence to virtual presence. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00AE1028"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>This shift has given rise to what might be called “virtual religiosity”—a form of religious practice mediated by digital technology and constructed through immersive experiences in virtual spaces. In practice, religious activities such as worship, religious study sessions, and community interactions can be represented in three-dimensional environments that resemble reality; in some cases, these environments are even capable of providing experiences that users perceive as “real.” Studies show that virtual reality technology is capable of creating a strong sense of presence, allowing individuals to feel emotional and spiritual engagement within these digital spaces.  This indicates that the metaverse functions not only as a communication medium but also as a new medium for religious experience. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00AE1028"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>Nevertheless, this transformation is not neutral; rather, it carries profound epistemological and theological implications. The process of dematerializing worship spaces has the potential to shift the meaning of sacredness from one originally grounded in physical space to one based on digital representation. In this context, physical presence   which has long been a crucial requirement in many religious practices   is beginning to be replaced by digital connectivity. Consequently, a fundamental question arises regarding the authenticity of religious experience: can  spiritual  experiences in virtual spaces hold the same value as those in physical  spaces? .  Furthermore, this phenomenon can be  analyzed  through the lens of Jean Baudrillard’s theory of simulation, which explains that in contemporary society, reality is increasingly replaced by simulations known as simulacra. In the context of the metaverse, virtual worship spaces can be understood as simulations of real worship spaces that not only represent but have the potential to replace the religious experience itself. As individuals interact more in virtual spaces than in physical ones, a shift toward hyperreality occurs   a condition where the boundary between reality and representation becomes blurred. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00AE1028"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">In this context, the metaverse cannot be understood merely as a neutral tool or medium, but rather as a technological structure that actively reshapes the way  humans understand and experience religion. In other words, technology not only facilitates religious practices but also reconstructs the very meaning of religiosity itself. This aligns with findings that the simulation of worship practices in the metaverse represents a form of religious adaptation to technology, yet it still leaves a tension between digital innovation and the underlying theological meaning.   Thus, the transformation from the mosque as a physical space to the metaverse as a virtual space indicates an ontological shift in Islamic religious practice, from one grounded in material presence to an experience mediated by technology. This shift opens new opportunities for expanded access and inclusivity, yet simultaneously presents serious challenges regarding authenticity, sacredness, and the sustainability of core values in religious practice in the digital age. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr></w:p><w:p w14:paraId="095057E6" w14:textId="34D5F14F" w:rsidR="00C15CB2" w:rsidRPr="00C15CB2" w:rsidRDefault="00AE1028" w:rsidP="00C15CB2"><w:pPr><w:pBdr><w:top w:val="nil"/><w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00AE1028"><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>Jean Baudrillard’s Theory of Simulation: Concepts, Stages, and Implications <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="num" w:pos="720"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00AE1028"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>Jean Baudrillard’s theory of simulation is one of the critical frameworks for understanding the transformation of reality in the modern and postmodern eras, particularly in the context of the dominance of media and digital technology. Baudrillard argues that in contemporary society, reality is no longer experienced directly, but rather through representations, signs, and simulations mass-produced by media and technological systems. In this context, humans live in a world filled with simulacra   representations or imitations that no longer refer to the original reality but stand on their own as a new reality.  Baudrillard distinguishes between representation and simulation: while representation still maintains a connection to the original reality, simulation erases the boundary between reality and representation. In simulation, signs no longer reflect reality but create their own reality. Therefore, simulacra are forms of representation that have lost their reference to the original reality and have become autonomous. In this context, humans no longer interact with “real” reality but with constructions of reality produced by the system of signs .   Baudrillard argues that simulation develops through several historical stages, namely: (1) The first stage (reflection of reality),  in which representations still directly reflect reality; (2) The second stage (masking reality), in which representations begin to obscure and modify reality; (3) The third stage (masking the absence of reality) is where representations conceal the absence of reality, so that only the construction is visible, (4). The fourth stage (pure simulacrum) is where representations are completely detached from reality and become reality itself; this final stage depicts a condition in which humans live in a world entirely constructed by simulation, without reference to the original reality. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="num" w:pos="720"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="009B2366"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>One of the key concepts in Baudrillard’s theory is hyperreality, a condition in which simulation feels more real than reality itself. In hyperreality, individuals are no longer able to distinguish between the real and the simulated, because simulation has replaced reality as the primary source of experience. A classic example given by Baudrillard is an amusement park or the mass media, but in a contemporary context, the metaverse and virtual reality represent the most cutting-edge forms of hyperreality.  Within the metaverse, human experience no longer depends on the physical world, but on digital constructs designed to create the illusion of presence. Users can experience social, emotional, and even spiritual interactions within a virtual space that is, in fact, a simulation. Thus, the metaverse can be understood as a concrete manifestation of hyperreality in the digital age. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="num" w:pos="720"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="009B2366"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Simulation theory has profound implications for our understanding of reality and knowledge. Ontologically, this theory challenges the assumption that reality is objective and stable, since in a simulated world, reality becomes a construct that can be reproduced and modified. Epistemologically, truth is no longer determined by correspondence with reality, but by consistency within the system of signs and the simulation itself. In a religious context, these implications are highly significant. If religious experiences can be reproduced through digital simulation, the question arises as to whether such experiences retain the same authenticity as those in the physical world. Religious practices in the metaverse have the potential to become a form of hyperreal religiosity, where spiritual experiences are no longer rooted in physical reality but in digitally designed simulations. Baudrillard’s theory becomes  highly relevant in  analyzing  the metaverse phenomenon because this technology directly embodies the concept of simulation in its most concrete form.   The metaverse creates a virtual world that not only represents reality but also replaces it as the primary space for human interaction. In this context, religion practiced in the metaverse is no longer merely transferred to a digital space but undergoes an ontological transformation, shifting from practices rooted in physical reality to those grounded in simulation. Thus, Baudrillard’s simulation theory provides a robust analytical framework for understanding how digital technology not only mediates but also reconstructs reality, including within the religious domain. This underscores that the metaverse is not merely a tool but a structure that reshapes human experience of reality, truth, and spirituality. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00603697"><w:t xml:space="preserve">Table 1. xml:space="preserve">The development of the metaverse and digital technology has brought significant changes to the structure of religious authority in Islam, particularly in the relationship between ulama as traditional authorities and digital platforms as new mediums for the production and distribution of religious knowledge. In classical tradition, religious authority is rooted in scholarly credibility,  sanad , and the community’s recognition of an ulama’s capacity to understand and interpret religious texts. This authority is hierarchical and institutionalized, where the position of an ulama is attained through a lengthy process of education, direct mentorship, and engagement within established scholarly networks. However, with  the emergence of digital spaces, this structure is undergoing a transformation toward a more open and decentralized model, where authority is no longer entirely monopolized by formal religious institutions. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="num" w:pos="720"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="009B2366"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>In this context, digital platforms such as social media, religious outreach apps, and even the metaverse enable individuals without formal authority to produce and disseminate religious interpretations to a wide audience. This phenomenon gives rise to what is known as digital religious authority   a form of authority built through visibility, popularity, and digital interaction, rather than solely based on traditional scholarly depth. Authority has become more fluid and competitive, as audiences have the freedom to choose sources of  authority  they deem relevant or engaging, unbound by the previously dominant hierarchical structures. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="num" w:pos="720"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="009B2366"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Furthermore, these changes have also impacted the issuance of  fatwas , particularly regarding contemporary issues such as virtual worship in the metaverse. Whereas fatwas were previously issued by official institutions using strict  usul  al- fiqh  methodologies, we now see the emergence of digital fatwas disseminated rapidly through online platforms, often without adequate collective deliberation. This creates a new dynamic in religious authority, where legitimacy is determined not only by scientific methodology but also by responsiveness and digital reach. In some cases, religious authority has even shifted from institutions to individuals with significant influence in the digital sphere . <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="num" w:pos="720"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00B33280"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>Further analysis shows that this decentralization of authority is not only driven by open access to information, but also by the role of algorithms in shaping the consumption of religious knowledge. Digital platforms use algorithms to recommend content based on user preferences, thereby indirectly shaping how individuals understand religion. In this context, algorithms function as “invisible curators” that determine which religious narratives become dominant, meaning that authority no longer rests entirely with religious scholars but is also influenced by technological logic and the attention economy.   The consequence of this phenomenon is the fragmentation of religious authority, where there is no longer a single dominant source of authority, but rather various competing authorities within  the digital space. On one hand, this opens opportunities for the democratization of religious knowledge and expands the public’s access to diverse perspectives. However, on the other hand, this situation also has the potential to cause epistemological disorientation, as not all available sources possess sufficient scientific validity. Therefore, the transformation of religious authority in the digital age must be understood as a complex phenomenon involving the interaction between Islamic scholarly traditions, digital technology, and contemporary social dynamics. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr></w:p><w:p w14:paraId="06C23E4E" w14:textId="422B7F97" w:rsidR="00325A61" w:rsidRPr="00186A89" w:rsidRDefault="00B33280" w:rsidP="00186A89"><w:pPr><w:pBdr><w:top w:val="nil"/><w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00B33280"><w:t>Table 2. w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>This article argues that the transformation of Islamic religious practices from the physical realm to the digital realm   particularly within the context of the metaverse and virtual reality   is not merely a change in medium, but rather a fundamental ontological and epistemological shift. By employing Jean Baudrillard’s theory of simulation, it becomes clear that religious practices in the metaverse tend to move from representation toward simulation, even reaching a state of hyperreality, where religious experiences no longer refer to physical reality  but to autonomous digital constructs. In this context, virtual worship not only replicates religious practices but has the potential to reshape the very meaning, experience, and authority of religion itself. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00EF02CA"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">From the perspective of  tur a ṯ , as emphasized by classical scholars such as Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, Imam al-Nawawi, and Ibn Taymiyyah, Islamic religious practice possesses a strong embodied dimension, in which physical presence, spatial connection, and the rituals of worship are integral to the validity and meaning of the worship itself. Furthermore, the thought of Ibn Khaldun and Ibn Jama’ah indicates that the social and epistemological dimensions of religion   such as solidarity (‘ aṣabiyyah ) and the transmission of knowledge   are highly dependent on direct interaction, which is difficult to fully replicate in a virtual space. Thus, religious practices in the metaverse tend to be reduced to symbolic and representational aspects, without fully embodying the ontological dimensions inherent in physical practices. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00EF02CA"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t>On the other hand, this development also has significant implications for the structure of religious authority. Authority, which was previously hierarchical and based on scholarly lineage, is now undergoing decentralization through the emergence of digital religious authority, where legitimacy is determined not only by scholarly competence but also by visibility and digital platform algorithms. This creates opportunities for the democratization of access to religious knowledge, but simultaneously poses risks of fragmentation of authority and epistemological disorientation among the faithful. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00EF02CA"><w:rPr><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Overall, this article concludes that the practice of Islam in the metaverse must be understood as an ambivalent phenomenon: on the one hand, it opens up opportunities for innovation, accessibility, and the global expansion of  da’wah ; on the other hand, it poses serious challenges to the authenticity, normative validity, and integrity of the religious experience. Therefore, a critical-integrative approach is needed that combines theoretical analysis, studies of the  turāṯ , and considerations of  maqāṣid  al- syarī‘ ah  to assess the extent to which technology can be accommodated without obscuring the fundamental principles of Islamic religious practice. Thus, the future of Islamic religiosity in the digital age does not lie in a substitution between the physical and the virtual, but rather in the ability to  negotiate both proportionally within a robust normative and epistemological framework. <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:ind w:firstLine="567"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr></w:p><w:p w14:paraId="59E52419" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00325A61" w:rsidRDefault="00000000"><w:pPr><w:pBdr><w:top w:val="nil"/><w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:line="360" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/></w:rPr><w:t>REFERENCES <w:left w:val="nil"/><w:bottom w:val="nil"/><w:right w:val="nil"/><w:between w:val="nil"/></w:pBdr><w:spacing w:before="300" w:after="300"/><w:jc w:val="both"/><w:rPr><w:color w:val="000000"/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="006F6DCC"><w:rPr><w:color w:val="000000"/><w:lang w:val="en-ID"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Al-Ghazali, A. w:val="18"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Source:  Source, 20 26 Result and Discussion The results should be clear and concise. They should  summarise  the (scientific) findings rather than presenting the data in detail. Please highlight the differences between your results or findings and previous publications by other researchers. The discussion should explore the significance of the research findings, rather than repeating them. A combined Results and Discussion section is often appropriate. Avoid extensive citations and discussion of published literature. In the discussion, this is the most important part of your article. Here you have the opportunity to present your data effectively. Ensure the discussion aligns with the results, but do not repeat them. It should often begin with a brief summary of the main scientific findings (not the experimental results). The following components must be covered in the discussion: (a) How do your results relate to the initial questions or objectives outlined in the Introduction? What are your research findings? (what / how)? (b) Do you provide a scientific interpretation for each result or finding presented? This scientific interpretation must be supported by valid  analysis and  characterisation  (why)? (c) Are your results consistent with what has been reported by other researchers (what else)? Or are there differences? Conclusion The conclusion should address only the research objectives. Explain how your research contributes to the advancement of the field from the current state of knowledge. Without a clear conclusion, reviewers and readers will find it difficult to evaluate the work and determine whether it is suitable for publication in the journal. Do not repeat the abstract or merely list the experimental results. Provide a clear scientific justification for your research, and highlight potential applications and further developments. This conclusion should be presented in paragraph form. You should also propose future experiments and/or mention ongoing experiments.  Acknowledgments Recognize those who helped in the research, especially funding supporter of your research References  Cite the main scientific publications on which your work is based. Cite only items that you have read. Do not inflate the manuscript with too many references. Avoid excessive self‐citations. Avoid excessive citations of publications from the same region. Check each reference against the original source (authors name, volume, issue, year). Please use Reference Manager Applications like EndNote, Mendeley, Zotero,  etc . and use APA 6th style . All publications cited in the text should be included as a list of references. Please ensure that every reference cited in the text is also present in the reference list (and vice versa).
